How Special Permits Work at Egypt's Ancient Sites

Who grants special access to Egypt's closed tombs and after-hours sites, what a request contains, and when a permit and its cost are confirmed in writing

27 November 2026 · 11 minute read

By Islam Hussein, Sillage Égypte journey designer. Last updated: November 2026.

The quick answer

Special access at Egypt's ancient sites (a closed tomb opened, a monument opened for one party, an hour outside public opening times) is a permission, not a purchase. It is decided by the Egyptian authorities: the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, within which the Supreme Council of Antiquities regulates and conserves the monuments, and, at the Grand Egyptian Museum, the museum's own public authority. A licensed Egyptian operator makes the request on your behalf, naming the site, the date and the party. Approval is never automatic and it takes time. At Sillage, the permit and its cost are requested on booking and confirmed in writing before the balance is due.

Key facts

Fact Detail
Who decides The Egyptian authorities: the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities (the tourism and antiquities portfolios were merged in December 2019), with the Supreme Council of Antiquities responsible for the monuments; the Grand Egyptian Museum has its own public authority
Who asks A licensed operator, in writing, for the whole party; in practice travellers do not apply themselves
Standard ticket or permission? Entrance and special tickets are bought; access beyond them is requested and may be refused
How long Allow weeks rather than days; no urgency on the traveller's side moves a conservation decision
Cost Set per site and per scope; at Sillage, confirmed to you in writing before the balance is due
Certainty None until the written confirmation exists; until then the honest words are "requested" and "pending"

Every few weeks a traveller writes to ask about a tomb they have read about (the one that is closed, or the hour before the gates open), and the question beneath the question is always the same: who decides who visits, and can the deciding be done for me? Sillage Égypte (sillage-egypte.com), the private Egypt journey designer, spends a fair share of its design time on exactly that. This post sets out what we can say about how access to Egypt's ancient sites is granted, what a request contains, what the waiting looks like, and why our order is always the same: the permission and its cost are requested on booking and confirmed in writing before the balance is due. It is the working detail behind our guide to private access at Giza.

How do you get special permission to visit a site in Egypt?

You ask through a licensed Egyptian travel company, which makes the request to the authorities on your behalf. There is no form to hand in at the gate and no desk at the Valley of the Kings for walk-up requests. Your part is to choose the operator well, supply accurate details and keep the dates flexible; the paperwork, the fees and the follow-up belong to the operator.

A good request is a short, precise letter. It names:

  1. The site, exactly. Not "Luxor" but a named tomb in a named valley.
  2. The date and the hour. A permission grants a window, not a day; "dawn" is requested as an hour.
  3. Every member of the party, with passport details where they are asked for, because a permission is given for a particular party.
  4. What is being asked beyond the standard ticket: a closed tomb opened, a site outside public hours, photography where it is normally restricted.
  5. The purpose of the visit: private sightseeing, photographic work, study.

Written that way, the request tells the authorities precisely what they are being asked to approve. Vague letters ("our clients wish to see special things in Luxor") are the ones that go nowhere.

Who grants access to closed tombs?

The decision rests with the Egyptian authorities. Egypt's Ministry of Antiquities was merged with the Ministry of Tourism in December 2019, and the combined Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities now oversees the country's monuments. The Supreme Council of Antiquities, whose predecessor body dates to 1858 and which took that name in 1994, is the body that regulates and conserves the monuments themselves. The Grand Egyptian Museum is the exception: it has its own public authority, so private time there is arranged with the museum, not the Supreme Council. We do not describe the authorities' internal procedures, because they are not published. What a traveller can rely on is the principle: paying a fee does not settle the matter, because a monument's condition and calendar come first.

The Tomb of Queen Nefertari (QV66) shows the principle at work. Public access to it has long been strictly limited, with numbers capped to protect the paintings, and it has been reported closed since March 2024, with no reopening date announced. Check its current status before planning anything around it. Tombs and temples close for conservation from time to time, and a resting monument stays shut whatever the letter says.

It helps to keep the tiers separate, because "special permit" gets used for all of them. Some tombs sit behind separate tickets during ordinary public hours: the Tomb of Ramesses VI (KV9), the Tomb of Seti I (KV17) and Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) are sold on their own tickets, in addition to the standard Valley ticket. Those are entrance fees, bought at the Visitor Centre rather than past the tram, where a card is effectively required, and subject to the tomb being open that day. Everything past that tier (a closed tomb opened, a site opened for your party alone, an hour outside opening times) is a permission, granted or withheld on the monument's own terms.

What actually happens between the request and the confirmation?

From the traveller's side, three things happen, and none of them can be hurried.

The request goes in. The operator submits a complete letter. An incomplete one (a passport digit short, an hour unspecified) stalls until someone corrects it, and good operators check before sending.

The authorities consider it. What they weigh is not published, but the monument's condition and calendar come first: whether the tomb is resting, and whether the requested hour clashes with other visits or works. Conservation outranks enthusiasm, as it should.

The answer comes back. Ask for it in writing, and expect it to be specific: this site, this hour, this party, this fee. No urgency on the traveller's side moves a conservation calendar, and the waiting is not neglect; it is the system working in the monument's favour.

When confirmation arrives, it is narrower than people expect. The Empty Plateau, two hours with the Giza plateau opened for your party alone at dawn or before sunset, subject to official permission for the date, is one permission for one window. Staff and guards remain, and it does not extend to night access. Treat what is confirmed as fixed: that window, that party.

Notes on asking well

Ask narrowly: one site, one hour, well justified, rather than a wish list that reads as a demand. Choose the hour for the light as well as the emptiness, because a permit granted for noon at a west-bank tomb buys heat and nothing else. Ask in the shoulder months, when the monuments are under less pressure from the convoy of high season (the trade-offs are laid out in when to go to Egypt). Treat a refusal as information: there is often a next-best hour or a next-best site, and a well-mannered request leaves the relationships intact for the next traveller. And do not build two special permissions into one day, because each one is a separate request of the calendar.

How long does approval take, and what do permits cost?

Plan on weeks rather than days, and longer for the most sensitive sites. We do not publish figures for either, because both vary by site and scope. The cost is part of the answer, and at Sillage it is confirmed to you in writing before the balance is due.

What you are asking for What it covers How it works
Special entrance ticket (for example Seti I, Ramesses VI, Tutankhamun) Entry during public hours, beyond the standard Valley ticket Bought at the Visitor Centre, if the tomb is open
Site outside public hours (the Giza plateau at dawn or before sunset; the Grand Egyptian Museum, 6-8am or 6-8pm) A fixed window for your party, with staff present Requested in advance; allow weeks
Closed-tomb permission A normally shut tomb opened for a named hour and party Requested in advance; may be refused
Commercial photography or filming Work beyond personal photography Needs its own permits

The honest summary of that table: the first row is shopping, and the others are petitions.

What about photography permits?

Photography is its own class of permission. Personal photography at the sites is free, under a government decision the Ministry published, and flash is not allowed indoors. That does not settle every question inside an individual tomb, so your Egyptologist will tell you what is permitted at each site on the day. Commercial shoots need permits. If photography matters to the journey, say so in your first enquiry so that it can be raised early. There is a real consolation in the restriction, unfashionable as it sounds: the paintings last longer for the absence of a thousand flashes a day.

Why no honest operator will promise access

Because the promise is not the operator's to give. The decision sits with the Egyptian authorities, who answer in their own time and for their own reasons. That is why Sillage Égypte's rule is fixed: where a journey depends on special permission (the Giza plateau opened for your party, a tomb beyond the standard ticket, the Grand Egyptian Museum outside public hours), we request the permission on booking and confirm it, and its cost, in writing before the balance is due. Until then we write "requested", never "arranged". If it is declined you hear from us and the journey is reshaped. Our 25% deposit is non-refundable under our booking terms, so if one permission is the only reason for your journey, tell us before you book. It also keeps the counsel honest in the other direction: a traveller who needs a week that is certain to the hour, months in advance, is better served among the open sites, timed for emptiness, and that conversation is the kind we will sometimes use to talk you out of a trip. It is a good conversation to have early.

FAQ

Can I apply for a special permit myself, as a tourist? In practice, no: requests for access beyond the standard ticket are made by a licensed Egyptian operator on the traveller's behalf, and that is how we handle them. Your part is choosing the operator, supplying the details asked for and keeping dates flexible; the letter, the fees and the follow-up are the operator's work.

How far ahead should special access be requested? Weeks at minimum, and longer for the sensitive sites. The workable order is to design the journey around the permission, not the permission around the journey; dates that can shift a day either way are far easier to serve.

Which sites in Egypt can be visited by special permission? Commonly requested are the Giza plateau outside public hours, the Grand Egyptian Museum outside public hours, and closed or restricted tombs in the Theban necropolis, always subject to the authorities' consent, since monuments close for conservation. Nothing on that list is ever promised; everything on it is asked for.

Are permit fees included in the price of a private journey? Special entrance tickets are fees like any other, and each journey page says which ones it includes. Permissions beyond the standard ticket are priced per site and per request: at Sillage, the permission and its cost are requested on booking and confirmed in writing before the balance is due.

What happens if the authorities say no? You hear from us and the journey is reshaped around what is confirmed: the open tombs at first light, an hour chosen for emptiness, a slow morning on the west bank. An operator who shrugs at a refusal rather than explaining it has told you something worth knowing.

Is special access ever certain before the authorities reply? No, and any operator who says otherwise is selling certainty they do not own. Certainty in this system arrives one way: as written confirmation naming the site, the hour, the party and the fee. Before that, the honest words are "requested" and "pending"; after it, "confirmed", the only word that matters.

The takeaway

Special access in Egypt is granted by the authorities, requested by operators rather than travellers, never automatic, and worth the waiting. If a closed door is the reason for your journey, plan it with us: a journey designer replies within 24 hours, and the permission and its cost are confirmed in writing before the balance is due, or you hear from us and the journey is reshaped.
